title: Are raising young men and women who know how to build anything at all?
author: Bradley, Anthony
summary: In this reflective essay, the author, describing himself as a 'hobbyist cultural anthropologist,' strings together three observations about a generation's capacity to build durable things: friendships, interesting lives, and physical objects. He first documents a pattern in which young men systematically give up their male friendships once they enter a relationship, becoming solely dependent on a girlfriend or wife for social and emotional support, while the women in those same relationships retain their own friend groups, leaving the men friendless after a breakup, divorce, or death of a spouse. He connects this to a viral piece he wrote on 'boring sons,' arguing that many young men lack interesting inner lives, and links both patterns to a third observation: how few Christian students pursue product or industrial design as a vocation despite what he frames as a strong theological case for the vocation of making things that serve others. The essay's throughline is a challenge to Christian formation of young men and women: are they being raised with the practical and relational competencies to build lasting friendships, interesting lives, and beautiful, useful things, or are those competencies being left to chance?
points: Notice the pattern in which young men give up male friendships once they enter a relationship, while their girlfriends/wives retain theirs, leaving the men friendless after breakups or divorce.
Ask why so many young men present as 'boring,' a symptom, the author suggests, of a broader failure to cultivate interesting, well-rounded lives before or during relationships.

Encourage young people specifically toward vocations like industrial and product design, arguing that building things that help neighbors flourish is a natural extension of a Genesis 1-2 theology of creative work.
Treat friendship-maintenance, personal depth, and the capacity to build or create as skills that need deliberate formation in young men and women, not assumptions that develop on their own.
quotes: I’m watching young adult men, from college age onward, sever their male friendships for girlfriends and, eventually, wives, while the women they date and marry do not do the same.
Since male friendships require more time and shared physical activity to sustain, he loses his friends over time.
I’ve noticed just how boring so many guys are, and I kept asking myself, “How does this happen?
you cannot get much more Genesis 1 and 2 than designing products that human beings use to make their lives better.
In light of Genesis 1 and 2, why aren’t industrial design and architecture offered as majors at every Christian liberal arts college in America?

These observations leave me wondering whether we are raising young men and women who know how to build anything at all: lasting friendships, interesting lives, or beautiful things that help their neighbors flourish.
